passage: In the pantry of the design studio, Chaitanya stared at her phone instead of her coffee. Overnight, strangers had found a clumsy post she wrote at nineteen and were calling her names, saying that was who she really was. She felt like nothing. Lalit, her team lead, found her there and pulled up a chair without saying a word. "They have one screenshot," Chaitanya said finally. "They don't have the rest of me." She wrote a single post correcting the one false detail about her old college, then muted the thread. Lalit walked her to lunch, and afterwards she called her sister from the stairwell. The storm was still on her screen, but by evening she was reading a client's email again.

qa.q: How old was Chaitanya when she wrote the post that strangers found?
How did Chaitanya feel about herself when she stared at her phone in the pantry?
qa.a: She felt worthless, as if the name-calling showed who she really was. Her later words, "They have one screenshot," show her starting to see that the mob knows only a fragment.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She corrected the one false detail once, then muted the thread, and she reached out to Lalit and her sister. That kept the noise out while she had support around her.

qa.q: How might Lalit have seen Chaitanya's situation when he sat down beside her?
qa.a: He seemed to see that she was hurting and chose company over a lecture, staying quiet and later walking her to lunch. 🤍

grounding: Strangers dig up a past post and cause shame; she remembers mobs act on fragments, corrects facts once, mutes, and seeks support.

passage:
"Don't read them," Ishita said, reaching for Kunal's phone.

"They found my college tweets," he said. "From when I was nineteen. The stupid joke about the hostel mess. Now they're saying I hate the cooks."

"Did you mean it that way?"

"No! But it doesn't matter. Someone called me garbage. Someone posted my old address."

Ishita sat on the arm of the sofa. "Kunal. They've read three lines of your life. They don't know you drove Amma to dialysis every week for two years."

"I feel like nothing."

"I know. Here's what we'll do. You write one line: the joke was old, badly worded, and you're sorry for how it sounds. One. Then mute everything."

"And then?"

"Then you call Dr. Mehra's counselling line like you did last year. And we watch old cricket matches until you sleep."

He typed the line. She took the phone and turned it face down.

qa.q: How old was Kunal when he wrote the college tweets?
What does Kunal's "I feel like nothing" show about how he feels?
qa.a: It shows he feels ashamed and worthless under the strangers' attacks.

qa.q: What was wise about Ishita's plan?
qa.a: She had Kunal correct the facts once, mute the attackers, and reach out to his counselling line, instead of arguing or reading more.

qa.q: How does Ishita see the mob's attack on Kunal?
qa.a: Ishita sees it as based on a fragment of his life, three old lines, not the person who drove Amma to dialysis every week.

grounding: The dialogue shows a young man attacked online over an old post who feels worthless, and his sister helping him correct the facts once, mute and seek support.

passage:
I'm Raghav. Two years ago, for about ten days, I was the most hated person on my city's internet.

I had reviewed a small café honestly, a bit harshly. The owner posted my review with my photo. By evening, people had found my school, my old girlfriend's comments, a blurry photo of me at a party at eighteen. Strangers called me a spoiled rich kid. I'm a bank clerk.

I stopped eating. I read every comment, believing each one.

My friend Anand came over on day three, took my phone, and said, "They're reading one page of a very long book."

That stuck. I posted one short correction: I'm not rich, the review was about the food, I'm sorry it came across so harsh. Then I muted everything and started seeing a counsellor.

By day ten, the storm had moved on to someone else. I hadn't.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel in the first days of the attack?
qa.a: Raghav felt worthless and ashamed, believing every comment and unable to eat.

qa.q: What steps helped Raghav get through it?
qa.a: Posting one short correction, muting everything, seeing a counsellor, and leaning on Anand's support.

qa.q: What would change if Anand had not come over?
qa.a: Raghav might have kept reading every comment alone, sinking deeper into shame without the reminder that the mob only saw a fragment.

grounding: The reflective account shows someone called names and having their past dug up online, feeling worthless, correcting facts once, muting and seeking support.
